narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it actually worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by two stronger negative signals.

Your LSAT score of 23 was the second most important factor and pulled the prediction sharply toward failure. Compared with the average score of 37 among students who were accepted, this was a substantial gap that significantly increased the model’s estimate of your risk.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.3 was the third most important driver and also pushed the outcome toward failure. It sits well below the 3.23 average of accepted students, reinforcing the model’s concern about your readiness for the bar exam.

Although your first-year grades, family income bracket, full-time status, gender, and race played smaller roles, they could not overcome the combined impact of the LSAT and undergraduate performance.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT. Strengthening these two areas would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
